chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Ubayd, from Abdullah ibn Musa, who said: Nasr ibn Ali narrated to us, from al-Nadr ibn Sinan, from Abu al-Rabi'ah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said:

The month of Ramadan is a month in which Allah, Exalted and Mighty, made fasting obligatory upon you. So whoever fasts it with faith and seeking reward, he will emerge from his sins as the day his mother gave birth to him.

key_terms.إِيمَاناً: With faith, indicating belief in the obligation and divine promise.
key_terms.ذُنُوبِهِ: His sins, the transgressions for which forgiveness is granted.
key_terms.رَمَضَانَ: Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, known for fasting.
key_terms.صِيَامَهُ: Its fasting, referring specifically to the obligatory fast of Ramadan.
key_terms.كَيَوْمَ: Like the day, a simile indicating a state of pure origin.
key_terms.وَاحْتِسَاباً: And seeking reward, indicating the intention to gain divine reward for the act.
key_terms.وَلَدَتْهُ: Gave birth to him, referring to the moment of birth when one is free from prior sins.

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward for fasting Ramadan with faith and sincerity?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this hadith from Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf underscores the theological link between ritual observance and spiritual purification, a cornerstone of Shia jurisprudence regarding the conditions of valid worship. The metaphor of returning to the state of a newborn (*kayawm waladat-hu ummahu*) signifies the erasure of minor sins, inviting believers to approach Ramadan with both *iman* (conviction) and *ihtisab* (anticipation of reward).
